title: Germline HLA and KIR Variation and Disease Control after Immune Checkpoint Blockade in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Exposure Definition Shapes the Signal
content: We examined germline HLA and KIR variation, typed from whole-exome sequencing, in 122 patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer treated with checkpoint inhibitors. In a screen of 448 tests, no association with the primary endpoint, unfavourable disease status at 3 months, reached q < 0.05. Nominally and and without surviving correction, HLA-A*02 carriers had higher odds of unfavourable status (odds ratio 4.00, 95% CI 1.64 to 10.07) and no HLA-B*14 carrier did (0 of 12; odds ratio 0.07, 0.0006 to 0.58). In 297 in-dependent patients cohort , B*14 was not supported (Cochran Q p = 0.027) and A*02 was inconclusive (Q p = 0.139). The only test below q = 0.05 was HLA-DQA1 evolutionary divergence at 12 months (odds ratio 0.42 per standard deviation, 0.23 to 0.70; q = 0.004 within its family, 0.299 across all tests). Divergence was bimodal and matched whether the two DQA1 alleles shared a first-field lineage: a two-group contrast, not a gradient. Grouping alleles changed the answer: the B27 supertype showed no association although B*14 did, and DQB1*03 showed none although DQB1*03:01 did (both nominal). Exome typing resolved HLA to allele group (99.1% of calls) but not KIR (19.0% ambiguous), so germline HLA can be recovered from exomes that already exist without additional se-quencing; DQA1 lineage structure is the hypothesis these data put forward for inde-pendent testing.
